bookCredit: The 1863 newspaper accounts and Sarah Bradford’s 1869 biography are in the public domain. Freedom Train by Dorothy Sterling (1954) is quoted only in short lines.
title: Three Tellings of One Night

banner.alt: A moonlit river with a steamboat and small boats pulling toward it, seen past a newsroom desk stacked with papers and books

keepsake.name: quilt square
keepsake.line: Only Imagination Trip travelers earn this one. Pieced from scraps, like Old Rit’s quilt.

body: One raid on the Combahee River, three writers. An unnamed reporter says near 800 were freed. Harriet’s own words say 756. Bradford, six years later, repeats Harriet.
Build a desk that holds all three.
postcard.word: A primary source was made at the time. A secondary source came later and used the primary ones.

mission.p: Lay the three accounts side by side, labeled A, B and C, with a clock for when.

steps.build:
Open your menu (top button, right controller) and click Models. Build in this order:
  1. the desk
  2. left: a newspaper under A (Wisconsin State Journal, 1863)
  3. middle: a newspaper under B (The Commonwealth, 1863)
  4. right: the book under C (Bradford, 1869), the clock beside it
steps.say: Stand at the desk like an editor. Practice these 2 sentences:
steps.frame: “Source ___ says ___, but Source ___ says ___. I trust ___ more because ___.”
steps.extra: Put a Handheld Microphone in front of the source you trust most.
steps.fits: the whole desk, A to C

points: Your video is 30 seconds or less, shows A, B and C on the desk with the clock, and you say 2 sentences: one fact two sources tell differently, and which you trust more and why.

alt.p: Tap the tellings of the raid in the order they happened, from the night itself to today.
alt.gameH: Tap the next one in time

events.t: The raid on the Combahee River
events.s: June 1863: the gunboats, the song, almost 800 aboard

events.t: An unnamed reporter writes it up
events.s: Wisconsin State Journal, 1863: a Black woman, near 800 freed
The Commonwealth, July 17, 1863: 756, and she is named
1869, six years later, reprinting Harriet’s letter

events.t: You lay all three side by side

alt.miss: Not yet. Ask which telling had to exist before this one could.

write.q: Pick one fact: how many people were freed, or what Harriet is called. In 2 sentences, say how two of the sources tell it differently, and which source you trust more and why.

scripts.brief: Hey, it’s Marcus. This week there is no new chapter. Instead you have three tellings of one night on the Combahee River: a newspaper that never names Harriet, a newspaper that prints her own words, and a biography written six years later. Build a newsroom desk that lays them side by side, A, B and C, with a clock for when each was written. Then tell me which one you trust most.
scripts.alt: No headset? Take the editor’s chair. Three writers told the story of the raid, and they told it at different times. Put the tellings in order, from the night itself to you at your desk today, and notice who had to go first.
scripts.saved: The desk is set, A to C. Here is your quilt square, the last one of the unit. Keep it, and remember that a story can be true three different ways.

testPara: Source A says near 800 were freed, but Source B says 756. I trust Source B more because Sanborn knew Harriet and printed her own words.
